title: Wrong Votes, Right Gradients: Why Majority-Vote Rewards Track Verifiable RL

paper.title: Wrong Votes, Right Gradients: Why Majority-Vote Rewards Track Verifiable RL
paper.abstract: Abstract Reinforcement learning with self-generated labels, such as majority vote over a model’s own samples, often recovers most of the gain of training with verifiable rewards. This is puzzling from the usual prompt-level view, in which majority vote only returns a model’s modal answer and cannot add information about correctness. We argue that the relevant unit is the batch-level update. Because parameters are shared, a prompt’s own gradient accounts for less than 1% of the change in that prompt’s output at practical batch sizes, so a wrong label matters only to the extent that label errors share a direction across prompts. We decompose the majority-vote update into shrinkage and misdirection relative to the gold update, and show that misdirection vanishes with batch size whenever errors are incoherent across prompts, however often the labels are wrong. Measuring per-response gradients on five models, we find that majority-vote errors are as incoherent as a random-reward null, that the majority-vote update agrees with the gold update as closely as two independent gold updates agree with each other, and that its noise-corrected cosine with the gold update is 1 within error. Randomly flipping up to 30% of gold labels leaves the update direction intact, while the same fraction flipped by a shared rule destroys it, and rewards that favor a kind of response on every prompt, such as a learned reward model, fall measurably short. The equivalence holds at every checkpoint we examine but is local: gold-reward training still ends ahead on held-out majority accuracy. Error coherence, not error rate, determines when self-generated labels can stand in for verification.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Reinforcement learning is increasingly used to post-train language models, and its most reliable form uses verifiable rewards: programs, proof checkers, or reference answers that decide whether an output is correct ( Shao et al., 2024 ; Guo et al., 2025 ; Zheng et al., 2026 ) . Verification also confines training to existing labeled data or to domains with an automatic oracle ( Zhao et al., 2026a ) . Self-generated rewards remove this constraint by deriving feedback from the model’s own outputs, such as agreement among sampled answers ( Zuo et al., 2026 ; Shafayat et al., 2025 ; Huang and others, 2026 ; Yu et al., 2025 ) , self-certainty ( Zhao et al., 2026b ) , or entropy ( Prabhudesai et al., 2025 ; Agarwal et al., 2026 ) . They often work surprisingly well: label-free training frequently recovers most of the improvement obtained with ground-truth rewards, and in some settings matches it ( Zuo et al., 2026 ; Shafayat et al., 2025 ; Zhao et al., 2026b ; Yu et al., 2026 ) (Table 10 ). Yet the same rewards can also improve and then collapse ( Shafayat et al., 2025 ; Zhang et al., 2025c ; Jin and others, 2026 ) , or reinforce a model’s existing preferences regardless of correctness ( He et al., 2026 ) . When do self-generated labels work, and why? The standard account is prompt-level ( He et al., 2026 ; Zhang et al., 2025a ) . For a fixed prompt, majority vote (MV) converges to the model’s modal answer, which need not be correct; it can sharpen the answer distribution but cannot extract correctness information that the distribution does not already contain. Several results sit uneasily with this account. TTRL raises the maj@64 of Qwen2.5-Math-7B on MATH-500 from 66.4 to 85.2, and its post-training average accuracy exceeds the initial maj@64 ( Zuo et al., 2026 , Fig. 7) . In our own runs, held-out problems whose majority answer is wrong acquire a correct majority at about three times the rate that resampling alone produces (Section 5 ). Both effects require information to move between problems, which a prompt-level account does not allow. We argue that the prompt is the wrong unit of analysis. Reinforcement learning sums reward-weighted gradients over a batch of diverse prompts and applies a single update to shared parameters. At practical batch sizes, a prompt’s own gradient accounts for less than 1% of the change in that prompt’s output, so a wrong label barely steers its own prompt; what matters is whether the errors of many wrong labels add up to a common direction. We make this precise by decomposing the MV update into a component along the gold update, which only rescales the step, and an orthogonal component, misdirection, which changes its direction (Section 4 ). Misdirection is governed by the coherence of label errors across prompts rather than by their rate. Incoherent errors vanish once the batch exceeds a critical size set by the coherence of the gold signal, however often the labels are wrong, whereas errors that share a direction leave a floor that no batch size removes. That independent noise averages out is familiar from supervised learning ( Rolnick et al., 2017 ; Chatterjee, 2020 ) ; what is new here is to apply it to the difference between two reward sources, to measure that difference directly in LLM post-training, and to turn it into a testable criterion for when self-generated labels can replace verification. We test this account with per-response gradient sketches, which let us evaluate any reward on the same samples. On five models from two families, the MV update agrees with the gold update as closely as two independent gold updates agree with each other, and after correcting for prompt-sampling noise its cosine with the gold update is 1 within error (Section 3 ). MV errors are as incoherent as a random-reward null, while gold gradients share a direction that dominates beyond a few dozen prompts. Controls behave as the account predicts. Randomly flipping up to 30% of gold labels leaves the update direction unchanged, whereas rewards that favor a kind of response on every prompt (frequent answers, confident answers, or those a learned reward model prefers) fall measurably short. The equivalence is local. It holds at every checkpoint we examine, but it does not make the two training runs identical: gold training still ends ahead on held-out majority accuracy, and MV training mainly sharpens single-sample answers (Section 5 ). Our results therefore give a criterion rather than a guarantee. Self-generated labels can stand in for verification when a model’s residual errors are sparse and specific to individual prompts, and they should fail where errors are shared, as with widely held misconceptions or prompts revisited until their errors accumulate.

sections.heading: Group-relative policy gradients.
sections.text: We train with GRPO ( Shao et al., 2024 ) . A training step draws B B prompts x 1 , … , x B x_{1},\dots,x_{B} and samples n n responses y i ​ 1 , … , y i ​ n y_{i1},\dots,y_{in} per prompt from the current policy π θ \pi_{\theta} . A reward r i ​ j ∈ { 0 , 1 } r_{ij}\in\{0,1\} scores each response, and its advantage is the reward relative to its group, A i ​ j = ( r i ​ j − r ¯ i ) / s i A_{ij}=(r_{ij}-\bar{r}_{i})/s_{i} , where r ¯ i \bar{r}_{i} is the group mean and s i s_{i} is either the group standard deviation or 1 1 . At the sampling policy the importance ratios equal one and clipping is inactive, so the update direction is a sum of per-prompt gradients, G ⁡ ( r ) = ∑ i = 1 B g i ​ ( r ) , g i ​ ( r ) = ∑ j = 1 n A i ​ j ​ ∇ θ ​ log ⁡ π θ ​ ( y i ​ j ∣ x i ) . G(r)=\sum_{i=1}^{B}g_{i}(r),\qquad g_{i}(r)=\sum_{j=1}^{n}A_{ij}\,\nabla_{\theta}\log\pi_{\theta}(y_{ij}\mid x_{i}). We call g i g_{i} the prompt gradient and G G the batch update.

sections.heading: Gold and majority-vote rewards.
sections.text: Both rewards compare the final answer a ⁡ ( y ) a(y) , taken from the last \boxed{} , with a target. The gold reward uses the reference answer, r i ​ j gold = 𝟏 [ a ( y i ​ j ) = a i ∗ ] r^{\mathrm{gold}}_{ij}=\mathbf{1}[a(y_{ij})=a^{\ast}_{i}] . The majority-vote (MV) reward uses the most frequent answer in the group, r i ​ j mv = 𝟏 [ a ( y i ​ j ) = a ^ i ] r^{\mathrm{mv}}_{ij}=\mathbf{1}[a(y_{ij})=\hat{a}_{i}] , and needs no label ( Zuo et al., 2026 ; Shafayat et al., 2025 ; Huang and others, 2026 ) . We write G mv G_{\mathrm{mv}} and G gold G_{\mathrm{gold}} for the two batch updates. When the majority answer is correct, a ^ i = a i ∗ \hat{a}_{i}=a^{\ast}_{i} , the two rewards coincide and so do the prompt gradients. The updates therefore differ only through prompts whose majority answer is wrong, E = G mv − G gold = ∑ i : a ^ i ≠ a i ∗ ( g i ( r mv ) − g i ( r gold ) ) , E=G_{\mathrm{mv}}-G_{\mathrm{gold}}=\sum_{i:\,\hat{a}_{i}\neq a^{\ast}_{i}}\big(g_{i}(r^{\mathrm{mv}})-g_{i}(r^{\mathrm{gold}})\big), which we call the MV error. A group in which every response receives the same gold reward has zero gold advantage, so no cosine with gold is defined on it; we use the groups that are mixed under gold (164 of 256 prompts on Qwen3-4B-Base). The filter is on gold alone and forced rather than chosen: MV is often still live on the excluded groups.

sections.heading: Models and training.
sections.text: Our main model is Qwen3-4B-Base ( Yang et al., 2025 ) , trained on DeepScaleR ( Luo et al., 2025 ) with B = 256 B=256 prompts and n = 16 n=16 responses per step. We train it twice from the same initialization, once with gold and once with MV rewards. Both runs see the same prompts at every step, so they differ only in the reward. Neither uses a KL or entropy term. For gradient analyses at initialization we add Qwen3-1.7B-Base, Qwen2.5-7B, Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct, and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct ( Grattafiori et al., 2024 ) . We evaluate on MATH-500 ( Hendrycks et al., 2021 ; Lightman et al., 2024 ) , including its 134 level-5 problems, with 64 samples per problem at temperature 1. Appendix A gives the full configuration.

sections.heading: Measuring updates.
sections.text: Comparing G mv G_{\mathrm{mv}} with G gold G_{\mathrm{gold}} requires both updates on the same responses. For every response we store the gradient of log ⁡ π θ ​ ( y i ​ j ∣ x i ) \log\pi_{\theta}(y_{ij}\mid x_{i}) at the sampling policy, compressed by a count sketch ( Charikar et al., 2002 ) to K = 2 16 K=2^{16} dimensions. Because g i g_{i} is linear in the advantages, the update under any reward is a reweighting of the same per-response sketches, so every reward we compare is evaluated on identical samples. Cosines computed from sketches agree with exact fp32 gradients to within 0.004 0.004 . Our analyses use mean-centered advantages ( s i = 1 s_{i}=1 ). Training divided by the group standard deviation; since s i s_{i} is a per-group scalar, recomputing under that weighting moves c ∞ c_{\infty} by at most 0.010 0.010 on any arm (Table 7 ).

sections.heading: Gold agreement as the benchmark.
sections.text: A cosine of one is the wrong benchmark: most of a prompt gradient is specific to that prompt, so even two gold updates on disjoint prompts are far from parallel. We therefore split the prompt groups into disjoint halves 𝒜 \mathcal{A} and ℬ \mathcal{B} and compute X = cos ⁡ ( G mv 𝒜 , G gold ℬ ) , Y = cos ⁡ ( G gold 𝒜 , G gold ℬ ) , Z = cos ⁡ ( G mv 𝒜 , G mv ℬ ) . X=\cos\!\big(G^{\mathcal{A}}_{\mathrm{mv}},G^{\mathcal{B}}_{\mathrm{gold}}\big),\qquad Y=\cos\!\big(G^{\mathcal{A}}_{\mathrm{gold}},G^{\mathcal{B}}_{\mathrm{gold}}\big),\qquad Z=\cos\!\big(G^{\mathcal{A}}_{\mathrm{mv}},G^{\mathcal{B}}_{\mathrm{mv}}\big). Y Y , the agreement of gold with itself, is the ceiling, and MV is as close to gold as the data can show when X ≈ Y X\approx Y ; pairing different halves keeps MV and gold from sharing sampling noise. If each half-batch update is its expectation plus independent prompt-sampling noise, the noise enters X X , Y Y , and Z Z only through their norms, so c ∞ = X Y ​ Z c_{\infty}=\frac{X}{\sqrt{YZ}} estimates the cosine between the expected MV and gold updates, which cos ⁡ ( G mv , G gold ) \cos(G_{\mathrm{mv}},G_{\mathrm{gold}}) approaches as the batch grows. This is the classical correction for attenuation ( Spearman, 1904 ) ; as a ratio of estimates, c ∞ c_{\infty} can exceed 1 by sampling error, although the cosine it estimates cannot. We average over random splits, bootstrap over prompt groups, and report c ∞ c_{\infty} only when Z ≥ 0.3 Z\geq 0.3 , below which it is unstable.

sections.heading: 3 Gradient-Level Comparison of Majority Vote and Gold
sections.text: We first ask how much the batch update changes when gold labels are replaced by MV. At initialization on all five models, it changes no more than prompt sampling already does; Section 5 follows training.

sections.heading: MV agrees with gold as well as gold agrees with itself.

sections.heading: Each prompt moves with the batch.
sections.text: Why does a wrong label cost so little? Because it barely steers its own prompt. On Qwen3-1.7B-Base, a small step along a prompt’s own gradient changes that prompt’s output only 1.7 to 1.9 times as much as a step along another prompt’s gradient (Table 18 ). Summed over a batch, the other prompts dominate: at B = 64 B=64 to 128 128 , a prompt’s own gradient accounts for 0.09–0.38% of the change in its output on the Qwen3 models, and 0.83% on Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct at B = 64 B=64 (Table 19 ). The batch also sets the direction of that change. On the 76 prompts in the first Qwen3-4B-Base training batch whose majority answer is wrong, the MV batch update still increases the expected gold reward on 82% of them, to first order. The prompt’s own mislabeled term contributes + 0.007 +0.007 to the cosine between the update and the prompt’s gold gradient; the other prompts contribute + 0.075 +0.075 , almost exactly as much as under gold labels ( + 0.074 +0.074 ). A wrong label is outvoted by the rest of the batch, so whether the MV update is right depends on how its errors add up across prompts.

sections.heading: 4 Why Label Errors Cancel
sections.text: Section 3 showed that the MV and gold updates point in the same direction in expectation. We now explain why, by separating two ways a label source can differ from gold and deriving when each survives a large batch.

sections.heading: 4.3 Error structure, not error rate
sections.text: Table 3 compares rewards whose errors differ in rate and structure, all on the same Qwen3-1.7B-Base responses. Independent flips isolate the error rate: as Corollary 1 predicts, c ∞ c_{\infty} stays at 1 for flip rates up to 30%, so a high error rate alone does not misdirect the update. Holding the rate fixed and changing only the structure separates the two. Flipping the same fraction by a rule shared across prompts, the longest correct and shortest incorrect responses, leaves the rate unchanged but makes the errors coherent ( ρ e \rho_{e} rises from the null, 0.2 0.2 – 1.4 × 10 − 3 1.4\times 10^{-3} , to 42 42 – 48 × 10 − 3 48\times 10^{-3} , above the gold gradients’ own 7.9 7.9 ). At a matched 20 % 20\% error rate random flips give c ∞ = 1.011 c_{\infty}=1.011 and shared-rule flips 0.287 0.287 ; at 31 % 31\% the shared-rule update points away from gold ( − 0.129 -0.129 ). The gap widens with ε \varepsilon while the random-flip column does not move; Figure 2 shows the same contrast on all six arms. The rewards that fall short favor a kind of response on every prompt. In expectation, random vote rewards each answer in proportion to its frequency, favoring frequent answers everywhere rather than only where the majority is wrong; self-certainty vote and INTUITOR favor confident answers; and an off-the-shelf reward model favors the responses it has learned to prefer, including confident ones ( Leng et al., 2025 ) . Each preference is a direction shared across prompts, and each interval lies below 1 (random vote 0.961, self-certainty vote 0.975, length-controlled INTUITOR 0.969, reward model 0.982). A pure length reward, whose error has the same direction on every prompt, points away from gold ( c ∞ = − 0.415 c_{\infty}=-0.415 ), and a reward with no signal stays near zero at every batch size (Figure 1 ). MV is the exception among the votes: it differs from gold only where the majority is wrong, and there its errors are specific to the prompt (Section 4.2 ). Length-controlled INTUITOR stays at 0.94–0.97 on the Qwen models but falls to 0.76–0.79 on the instruction-tuned Llama models (Table 15 ), although model family and instruction tuning are confounded here. sections.heading: 5 Training Dynamics
sections.text: Sections 3 and 4 compare updates at fixed parameters, but training changes the model and with it the errors that MV makes. Following the gold and MV runs of Qwen3-4B-Base, which see identical prompts at every step, we ask whether the property behind the equivalence survives training, and whether equivalence at each step makes the two runs end in the same place. Answer parsing degrades slowly rather than failing: the parseable fraction falls from 0.84 0.84 at step 8 to 0.75 0.75 at step 20 while the majority answer’s accuracy stays flat, and what moves monotonically is the concentration of the vote (Appendix A ). We therefore report step 20 throughout.

sections.heading: The runs track each other on the training distribution.
sections.text: Evaluated on both runs, the MV reward rises almost as fast in the gold run as in the run that optimizes it (Figure 4 , Appendix C ), because the two rewards coincide wherever the majority is correct. Training accuracy is indistinguishable through step 15 (prompt-paired difference + 0.002 +0.002 [ − 0.001 -0.001 , + 0.006 +0.006 ] over 3,840 pairs). The runs differ in the weight placed on wrong majorities: the gap between MV reward and accuracy grows from 0.09 to 0.15 in the MV run but stays at 0.09 to 0.10 in the gold run.

sections.heading: MV repairs wrong majorities through other prompts.
sections.text: Of the 134 level-5 MATH-500 problems, 66 have a wrong majority under the base model; by step 20 of the MV run, 13 of them (19.7%) have a correct one (Table 14 ), about three times the flip rate between two independent halves of the samples. Since the run does not train on these problems, the repair comes from the shared update. Breakage runs at 4.4%, below the resampling rate. The gains are largest at small k k , where maj@1 and maj@4 rise by 17 to 19 points, but maj@16 and maj@64 rise significantly too ( + 0.100 +0.100 and + 0.082 +0.082 ). MV training changes the answer the model commits to on a single sample more than it changes the vote. The evaluation problems are all but disjoint from training: against the 29k DeepScaleR problems, one level-5 problem appears verbatim and two more exceed a 0.80 0.80 token-overlap threshold (Appendix A ). Dropping all three leaves the repair rate inside its interval.

sections.heading: Local equivalence does not make the trajectories identical.
sections.text: On held-out problems, gold training ends ahead. At step 10 on the level-5 problems, averaging over two seeds per reward, gold leads MV in maj@1 (0.344 vs. 0.320) and maj@64 (0.590 vs. 0.541), though not in pass@64 (0.855 vs. 0.862); on all of MATH-500 at step 20, maj@64 rises from 0.747 to 0.772 with MV and to 0.845 with gold. Doubling the MV batch to 512 prompts does not close the gap (step-10 maj@64 0.545 0.545 vs. 0.582 0.582 , paired 95% CI [ − 0.007 , + 0.086 ] [-0.007,+0.086] ), as expected when 256 prompts is already far above B ∗ B^{\ast} , so the gap must come from something that per-step misdirection does not capture. Labels must also come from the current policy: labels from the frozen base model are nearly as accurate as on-policy MV but deliver far less of the gold update (Appendix C ). Paired over the 500 problems, MV’s gain over base is significant at every k k but collapses with it, from + 0.237 +0.237 [ + 0.223 +0.223 , + 0.252 +0.252 ] at maj@1 to + 0.026 +0.026 [ + 0.005 +0.005 , + 0.047 +0.047 ] at maj@64, against + 0.262 +0.262 and + 0.099 +0.099 for gold. At step 10 gold’s advantage is weaker than the spread between seeds (Table 8 ). The property behind the equivalence thus persists through training, yet the runs separate on held-out majority accuracy: equivalence at each step bounds the error an update adds, not how errors accumulate (Section 7 ).

sections.heading: Self-generated rewards.
sections.text: Models can improve from their own outputs, by fine-tuning on self-consistent answers ( Huang et al., 2023 ; Wang et al., 2023 ) or by judging their own responses ( Yuan et al., 2024 ; Li et al., 2026c ) ; see Tao et al. (2024) and Tan et al. (2024) for surveys. In RL for reasoning, the reward can come from majority vote ( Zuo et al., 2026 ; Shafayat et al., 2025 ) , from confidence or entropy ( Kang et al., 2025 ; Zhao et al., 2026b ; Huang et al., 2026a ; Prabhudesai et al., 2025 ; Agarwal et al., 2026 ; Zhang et al., 2025b ) , or from stabilized variants ( Zhou et al., 2025 ; Zhang et al., 2025d ; Yu et al., 2026 ) . Self-play systems also generate the tasks themselves ( Huang and others, 2026 ; Yu et al., 2025 ; Chen et al., 2025 ; Huang et al., 2026b ; Huang et al., 2026e ; Yang et al., 2026 ; Zhao et al., 2026a ; Liu et al., 2026 ; Liu et al., 2025 ; Yue et al., 2026 ; Shi et al., 2026 ; Huang et al., 2026c ; He et al., 2025 ; Li et al., 2026a ; Li et al., 2026b ) , sometimes with checks on the generated data ( Lai et al., 2026 ; Shen et al., 2026 ; Liang et al., 2026 ) . Rather than propose a new reward, we explain when such rewards can replace verification.

sections.heading: Label-free reinforcement learning.
sections.text: When label-free training works remains unsettled ( Rahman et al., 2026 ; He et al., 2026 ) . It can collapse ( Shafayat et al., 2025 ; Zhang et al., 2025c ; Jin and others, 2026 ) , reinforce the model’s own preferences ( He et al., 2026 ; Arazo et al., 2020 ) , or lose the correct answer when the consensus is wrong ( Lin et al., 2026 ) , which has motivated complementary signals and verifiers ( Yan et al., 2026 ; Pan et al., 2026 ; Wang et al., 2025a ; Liao et al., 2026 ) . Gains can also come from spurious rewards or contamination ( Shao and others, 2025 ; Chen and others, 2025 ; Wu and others, 2025 ) , and RL may mostly sharpen existing behavior unless exploration is broadened ( Yue and others, 2025 ; Huang et al., 2026d ) . Existing explanations are prompt-level ( He et al., 2026 ; Zhang et al., 2025a ) . Ours is batch-level: in the spirit of label-noise robustness ( Rolnick et al., 2017 ) and shared gradient directions ( Chatterjee, 2020 ; McCandlish et al., 2018 ; Wei et al., 2026 ) , it asks whether the error between two reward sources has a shared component.

sections.heading: 7 Conclusion and Limitations
sections.text: We have argued that the batch-level update, not the individual prompt, is the right unit for understanding self-generated rewards. A fixed policy can have a wrong modal answer on a given problem, and MV will return it; but reinforcement learning updates shared parameters from many diverse prompts, and a wrong label matters only when errors across a batch share a direction. In our measurements they do not: a pretrained model’s residual errors are sparse and prompt-specific, stay incoherent across prompts at every checkpoint we measure, and cancel in aggregate, while structure shared across prompts is reinforced. The same view clarifies what verification adds. With any reward, GRPO improves only behavior that can be expressed as a coherent change to one shared policy, so the advantage of verifiable over self-generated labels should be largest for errors that recur across many prompts: in domains with widely shared misconceptions ( Lin et al., 2022 ; Prelec et al., 2017 ) , or when the same prompts are revisited until their errors accumulate. For label-free methods, the criterion suggests that making errors incoherent, by labelling with the current policy (Appendix C ) and drawing fresh and diverse prompts, matters as much as making them rare.

sections.heading: Limitations.
sections.text: Our training runs use one model, Qwen3-4B-Base, and Qwen models benefit even from rewards unrelated to correctness ( Shao and others, 2025 ) ; only the gradient-level results cover five models from two families. The runs are short and unregularized, and beyond step 15 the MV run’s entropy rises sharply, a regime we do not analyze. We have two runs per reward and measure cosines of raw gradients, whereas Adam’s preconditioner can reweight directions. Most importantly, per-step equivalence does not establish equivalence of trajectories, and over the nine steps we measure the errors already accumulate slightly faster than a random walk (Section 4.4 ).

sections.heading: Reproducibility Statement
sections.text: Appendix A lists the training configuration, prompt format, evaluation protocol, and gradient-sketch procedure, and Appendix B gives all proofs. We will release, under an open licence: the gradient-sketching code and the count-sketch implementation; the reward-reweighting, split-half and disattenuation estimators that produce every number in this paper; the scripts that generate each table and figure; and the launcher and configuration files for every training and evaluation run, including the majority-vote advantage estimator. We will also release the per-response gradient sketches, the gold and majority-vote label sets, the full text of every generation used in the analyses rather than extracted answers alone, and the dated experiment log recording each run’s configuration, failures, and diagnosed causes, so that both the reported analyses and the path taken to them can be reproduced.

sections.heading: Prompt format and answer extraction.
sections.text: Prompts use the Qwen chat template with the system prompt “Please reason step by step, and put your final answer within \boxed{} .” Thinking mode is disabled, so the response begins with an empty thinking block. The answer of a response is the content of the last \boxed{} in its final 400 characters. A response whose answer cannot be parsed takes no part in the vote and receives reward 0; ties are broken toward the answer that appears first in the group. The training reward and the reward applied to the stored sketches use the same rule.

sections.heading: Evaluation–training overlap.
sections.text: We checked all 500 MATH-500 problems against the 29,000 DeepScaleR training problems under three tests: equality of whitespace- and L a T e X -normalised strings, substring containment in either direction, and token-set Jaccard overlap at a 0.80 threshold. One problem matches exactly and 22 exceed the overlap threshold; restricted to the 134 level-5 problems used in Section 5 , the counts are one exact and two near matches. The detector was validated by planting verbatim and reformatted copies of training problems into the evaluation set, all of which it recovered. Excluding the three flagged level-5 problems changes the wrong-to-right majority repair rate by less than its bootstrap interval.

sections.heading: Gradient sketches.
sections.text: For each response we compute the gradient of log ⁡ π θ ​ ( y ∣ x ) \log\pi_{\theta}(y\mid x) , summed over response tokens, at the policy that generated it, and compress it with a count sketch to K = 2 16 K=2^{16} dimensions (fixed hash seed). The group gradient under a reward is ∑ j ( r i ​ j − r ¯ i ) ​ s i ​ j \sum_{j}(r_{ij}-\bar{r}_{i})\,s_{ij} , where s i ​ j s_{ij} is the sketch of response j j . A checkpoint from step t t is sketched on the responses the run generated at step t + 1 t+1 , so the sketches are on-policy. For Qwen3-4B-Base each checkpoint yields 256 × 16 256\times 16 responses. Qwen3-1.7B-Base is sketched on 1536 prompts and the two Llama models on 512 fresh DeepScaleR prompts, with 16 responses each. Qwen2.5-7B is sketched on 256 prompts with 16 responses each. The pooled Qwen3-4B arm of 512 prompts combines two batches of 256, the second generated after one update, so half of it is off-policy; the on-policy row of Table 1 is the first batch alone, and every result we draw conclusions from is reported for that row as well. Cosines from sketches agree with exact fp32 gradients to within 0.0039 0.0039 .

sections.heading: Groups with no gold signal.
sections.text: Section 2 restricts the comparisons to groups that are mixed under the gold reward, because a group whose responses all receive the same gold reward contributes the zero vector to G gold G_{\mathrm{gold}} and admits no cosine with it. MV is frequently still live on the excluded groups, so the restriction is not neutral for the MV side. Repeating the Qwen3-4B-Base comparison over all 256 prompts rather than the 164 mixed ones leaves the disattenuated cosine unchanged ( c ∞ = 0.985 c_{\infty}=0.985 , 95% CI [ 0.940 , 1.073 ] [0.940,1.073] , against 0.999 0.999 [ 0.965 , 1.043 ] [0.965,1.043] ) while raising the norm ratio ‖ G mv ‖ / ‖ G gold ‖ \|G_{\mathrm{mv}}\|/\|G_{\mathrm{gold}}\| from 1.14 1.14 to 1.62 1.62 and the misdirection R ⟂ R_{\perp} from 0.43 0.43 to 0.75 0.75 . Including the gold-silent groups therefore makes the MV update larger without turning it: the extra mass has no gold counterpart to align with, which is what a group carrying MV signal and no gold signal must contribute.

Wilson Affiliation: Dartmouth College Email: dylan.p.wilson.27@dartmouth.edu Chengsong Huang Affiliation: Washington University in St. Louis Email: chengsong@wustl.edu Jiaxin Huang Affiliation: Washington University in St. Louis Email: jiaxinh@wustl.edu Abstract Reinforcement learning with self-generated labels, such as majority vote over a model’s own samples, often recovers most of the gain of training with verifiable rewards. This is puzzling from the usual prompt-level view, in which majority vote only returns a model’s modal answer and cannot add information about correctness. We argue that the relevant unit is the batch-level update. Because parameters are shared, a prompt’s own gradient accounts for less than 1% of the change in that prompt’s output at practical batch sizes, so a wrong label matters only to the extent that label errors share a direction across prompts. We decompose the majority-vote update into shrinkage and misdirection relative to the gold update, and show that misdirection vanishes with batch size whenever errors are incoherent across prompts, however often the labels are wrong. Measuring per-response gradients on five models, we find that majority-vote errors are as incoherent as a random-reward null, that the majority-vote update agrees with the gold update as closely as two independent gold updates agree with each other, and that its noise-corrected cosine with the gold update is 1 within error. Randomly flipping up to 30% of gold labels leaves the update direction intact, while the same fraction flipped by a shared rule destroys it, and rewards that favor a kind of response on every prompt, such as a learned reward model, fall measurably short. The equivalence holds at every checkpoint we examine but is local: gold-reward training still ends ahead on held-out majority accuracy. Error coherence, not error rate, determines when self-generated labels can stand in for verification. Code: https://github.com/dylan518/wrong-votes-right-gradients 1 Introduction Reinforcement learning is increasingly used to post-train language models, and its most reliable form uses verifiable rewards: programs, proof checkers, or reference answers that decide whether an output is correct ( Shao et al., 2024 ; Guo et al., 2025 ; Zheng et al., 2026 ) . Verification also confines training to existing labeled data or to domains with an automatic oracle ( Zhao et al., 2026a ) . Self-generated rewards remove this constraint by deriving feedback from the model’s own outputs, such as agreement among sampled answers ( Zuo et al., 2026 ; Shafayat et al., 2025 ; Huang and others, 2026 ; Yu et al., 2025 ) , self-certainty ( Zhao et al., 2026b ) , or entropy ( Prabhudesai et al., 2025 ; Agarwal et al., 2026 ) . They often work surprisingly well: label-free training frequently recovers most of the improvement obtained with ground-truth rewards, and in some settings matches it ( Zuo et al., 2026 ; Shafayat et al., 2025 ; Zhao et al., 2026b ; Yu et al., 2026 ) (Table 10 ). Yet the same rewards can also improve and then collapse ( Shafayat et al., 2025 ; Zhang et al., 2025c ; Jin and others, 2026 ) , or reinforce a model’s existing preferences regardless of correctness ( He et al., 2026 ) . When do self-generated labels work, and why? The standard account is prompt-level ( He et al., 2026 ; Zhang et al., 2025a ) . For a fixed prompt, majority vote (MV) converges to the model’s modal answer, which need not be correct; it can sharpen the answer distribution but cannot extract correctness information that the distribution does not already contain. Several results sit uneasily with this account. TTRL raises the maj@64 of Qwen2.5-Math-7B on MATH-500 from 66.4 to 85.2, and its post-training average accuracy exceeds the initial maj@64 ( Zuo et al., 2026 , Fig. 7) . In our own runs, held-out problems whose majority answer is wrong acquire a correct majority at about three times the rate that resampling alone produces (Section 5 ). Both effects require information to move between problems, which a prompt-level account does not allow. We argue that the prompt is the wrong unit of analysis. Reinforcement learning sums reward-weighted gradients over a batch of diverse prompts and applies a single update to shared parameters. At practical batch sizes, a prompt’s own gradient accounts for less than 1% of the change in that prompt’s output, so a wrong label barely steers its own prompt; what matters is whether the errors of many wrong labels add up to a common direction. We make this precise by decomposing the MV update into a component along the gold update, which only rescales the step, and an orthogonal component, misdirection, which changes its direction (Section 4 ). Misdirection is governed by the coherence of label errors across prompts rather than by their rate. Incoherent errors vanish once the batch exceeds a critical size set by the coherence of the gold signal, however often the labels are wrong, whereas errors that share a direction leave a floor that no batch size removes. That independent noise averages out is familiar from supervised learning ( Rolnick et al., 2017 ; Chatterjee, 2020 ) ; what is new here is to apply it to the difference between two reward sources, to measure that difference directly in LLM post-training, and to turn it into a testable criterion for when self-generated labels can replace verification. We test this account with per-response gradient sketches, which let us evaluate any reward on the same samples. On five models from two families, the MV update agrees with the gold update as closely as two independent gold updates agree with each other, and after correcting for prompt-sampling noise its cosine with the gold update is 1 within error (Section 3 ). MV errors are as incoherent as a random-reward null, while gold gradients share a direction that dominates beyond a few dozen prompts. Controls behave as the account predicts. Randomly flipping up to 30% of gold labels leaves the update direction unchanged, whereas rewards that favor a kind of response on every prompt (frequent answers, confident answers, or those a learned reward model prefers) fall measurably short. The equivalence is local. It holds at every checkpoint we examine, but it does not make the two training runs identical: gold training still ends ahead on held-out majority accuracy, and MV training mainly sharpens single-sample answers (Section 5 ). Our results therefore give a criterion rather than a guarantee. Self-generated labels can stand in for verification when a model’s residual errors are sparse and specific to individual prompts, and they should fail where errors are shared, as with widely held misconceptions or prompts revisited until their errors accumulate. 2 Preliminaries Group-relative policy gradients. Models can improve from their own outputs, by fine-tuning on self-consistent answers ( Huang et al., 2023 ; Wang et al., 2023 ) or by judging their own responses ( Yuan et al., 2024 ; Li et al., 2026c ) ; see Tao et al. (2024) and Tan et al. (2024) for surveys. In RL for reasoning, the reward can come from majority vote ( Zuo et al., 2026 ; Shafayat et al., 2025 ) , from confidence or entropy ( Kang et al., 2025 ; Zhao et al., 2026b ; Huang et al., 2026a ; Prabhudesai et al., 2025 ; Agarwal et al., 2026 ; Zhang et al., 2025b ) , or from stabilized variants ( Zhou et al., 2025 ; Zhang et al., 2025d ; Yu et al., 2026 ) . Self-play systems also generate the tasks themselves ( Huang and others, 2026 ; Yu et al., 2025 ; Chen et al., 2025 ; Huang et al., 2026b ; Huang et al., 2026e ; Yang et al., 2026 ; Zhao et al., 2026a ; Liu et al., 2026 ; Liu et al., 2025 ; Yue et al., 2026 ; Shi et al., 2026 ; Huang et al., 2026c ; He et al., 2025 ; Li et al., 2026a ; Li et al., 2026b ) , sometimes with checks on the generated data ( Lai et al., 2026 ; Shen et al., 2026 ; Liang et al., 2026 ) . Rather than propose a new reward, we explain when such rewards can replace verification. Label-free reinforcement learning. When label-free training works remains unsettled ( Rahman et al., 2026 ; He et al., 2026 ) . It can collapse ( Shafayat et al., 2025 ; Zhang et al., 2025c ; Jin and others, 2026 ) , reinforce the model’s own preferences ( He et al., 2026 ; Arazo et al., 2020 ) , or lose the correct answer when the consensus is wrong ( Lin et al., 2026 ) , which has motivated complementary signals and verifiers ( Yan et al., 2026 ; Pan et al., 2026 ; Wang et al., 2025a ; Liao et al., 2026 ) . Gains can also come from spurious rewards or contamination ( Shao and others, 2025 ; Chen and others, 2025 ; Wu and others, 2025 ) , and RL may mostly sharpen existing behavior unless exploration is broadened ( Yue and others, 2025 ; Huang et al., 2026d ) . Existing explanations are prompt-level ( He et al., 2026 ; Zhang et al., 2025a ) . Ours is batch-level: in the spirit of label-noise robustness ( Rolnick et al., 2017 ) and shared gradient directions ( Chatterjee, 2020 ; McCandlish et al., 2018 ; Wei et al., 2026 ) , it asks whether the error between two reward sources has a shared component. 7 Conclusion and Limitations We have argued that the batch-level update, not the individual prompt, is the right unit for understanding self-generated rewards. A fixed policy can have a wrong modal answer on a given problem, and MV will return it; but reinforcement learning updates shared parameters from many diverse prompts, and a wrong label matters only when errors across a batch share a direction. In our measurements they do not: a pretrained model’s residual errors are sparse and prompt-specific, stay incoherent across prompts at every checkpoint we measure, and cancel in aggregate, while structure shared across prompts is reinforced. The same view clarifies what verification adds. With any reward, GRPO improves only behavior that can be expressed as a coherent change to one shared policy, so the advantage of verifiable over self-generated labels should be largest for errors that recur across many prompts: in domains with widely shared misconceptions ( Lin et al., 2022 ; Prelec et al., 2017 ) , or when the same prompts are revisited until their errors accumulate. For label-free methods, the criterion suggests that making errors incoherent, by labelling with the current policy (Appendix C ) and drawing fresh and diverse prompts, matters as much as making them rare. Limitations. Our training runs use one model, Qwen3-4B-Base, and Qwen models benefit even from rewards unrelated to correctness ( Shao and others, 2025 ) ; only the gradient-level results cover five models from two families. The runs are short and unregularized, and beyond step 15 the MV run’s entropy rises sharply, a regime we do not analyze. We have two runs per reward and measure cosines of raw gradients, whereas Adam’s preconditioner can reweight directions. Most importantly, per-step equivalence does not establish equivalence of trajectories, and over the nine steps we measure the errors already accumulate slightly faster than a random walk (Section 4.4 ).
